dimension_justifications.soundness: T1 and T3 are correct under their displayed assumptions. T2's proof invokes ambient matrix bounds on every segment-average Hessian, but the stated segmentwise strong-convexity/smoothness assumptions do not explicitly supply those bounds; under the natural restricted-segment reading, the full-norm contraction need not hold.
dimension_justifications.presentation: The manuscript clearly separates T1--T3, states important scope exclusions, and presents concise proofs. The T2 assumption-to-proof gap and the connection from generic contractions to a training-path intervention remain insufficiently specified.
dimension_justifications.contribution: The verified results are elementary product/contraction facts. As written, they do not establish a quantitative dependence of a trajectory on an intervention block or compare an intervened path with a clean/reference path, so the title-level training-path framing is not yet supported by the formal results.

paper_summary: The submission gives three scoped formal statements: a fixed-quadratic gradient-descent product identity with a log-remainder bound (T1), clean-tail full-norm and conditional directional contraction after switching objectives (T2), and an affine scalar conditional-mean product law (T3). It deliberately makes no empirical or deployment claim.
strongest_verified_contribution: T1's exact fixed-Hessian product identity and finite-step log-contraction remainder are self-contained and correct under the stated stability condition; T3's expectation recursion is likewise correct for the explicitly assumed affine process.
strengths: T1 correctly preserves the finite-step squared-step remainder instead of equating schedules merely from equal exposure.
T3 appropriately states the affine conditional-zero-mean recursion as a premise rather than claiming it for nonlinear or shuffled SGD.
The manuscript explicitly limits its conclusions to the assumptions of each theorem and avoids unsupported empirical transfer.
questions: In T2, do “mu-strongly convex and L-smooth on every segment” mean the explicit ambient matrix bounds mu I <= nabla^2 L_A(w_A^star+r(w_t-w_A^star)) <= L I for every relevant t and r? If so, please state them directly.
What theorem quantitatively links an intervention block D to a changed iterate or to a reference clean trajectory, rather than only contracting an arbitrary post-switch state w_s toward w_A^star?

Is the intended contribution a collection of elementary scoped lemmas, or a new intervention-comparison result? The title and introduction currently suggest the latter while T1--T3 establish the former.

issues.location: Paper p. 2, Section 3.2, Theorem T2 assumptions (lines 127-145 of source) and proof sentence “The assumed Hessian bounds imply” (lines 156-163).
issues.observed_evidence: T2 states that L_A is mu-strongly convex and L-smooth “on every segment joining a tail iterate” to w_A^star, but its proof requires the stronger ambient spectral statement mu I <= Hbar_t <= L I. Segmentwise scalar curvature/value conditions do not in general bound the off-segment component of Hbar_t(w_t-w_A^star), so they do not justify the spectral-norm step. For example, for a one-step tail from (1,0) toward 0, the quadratic L(x,y)=0.5x^2+Kxy+0.5(K^2+1)y^2 is globally strongly convex and has gradient Lipschitz constant sqrt(1+K^2) along that segment, yet a step eta=1/sqrt(1+K^2) produces a substantial orthogonal component and violates the asserted full-norm bound for large K.
issues.why_it_matters: This is the central proof step for T2. Without an explicit ambient Hessian bound along the relevant segments, the advertised clean-tail full-parameter return theorem is not established.
issues.required_fix: State the required condition explicitly as mu I <= nabla^2 L_A(w_A^star+r(w_t-w_A^star)) <= L I for every relevant t and r in [0,1], or replace the spectral-norm argument with a valid bound under a demonstrably weaker assumption. Update the abstract and limitations to match the corrected premise.
issues.verification_test: Independently check that the revised assumptions imply mu I <= Hbar_t <= L I by integration and then rederive the norm bound. Also test the displayed quadratic counterexample against the old wording and confirm that the revised premise excludes it.
issues.evidence_needed: A corrected self-contained theorem statement and proof; no empirical evidence is needed.

issues.location: Paper p. 1, Abstract and Introduction paragraphs beginning “when an objective is changed along a training trajectory”; p. 2, Sections 3.1--3.2; p. 3, Section 7 conclusion.
issues.observed_evidence: T1 varies only a learning-rate schedule on one fixed quadratic, T3 assumes a generic scalar affine recursion, and T2 contracts an arbitrary switched-in state w_s toward w_A^star. None defines an objective containing D, a reference trajectory, or a bound on the difference caused by inserting/removing D. Thus the results do not themselves yield a training-path intervention dependence or a clean-tail “return” relative to a prior/reference path.
issues.why_it_matters: The intervention/training-path framing is the paper's stated problem and title. Generic contraction after a switch does not quantify the intervention's effect, so the central interpretation exceeds the demonstrated formal consequences.
issues.required_fix: Either narrow the title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion to elementary scoped contraction identities, or add a theorem that defines an intervened and a reference path and bounds their difference using explicit assumptions on the objective change and tail dynamics.
issues.verification_test: For a revised intervention theorem, instantiate a fixed quadratic with a nonzero intervention gradient and verify algebraically that the claimed bound controls the intervened-versus-reference iterate difference. For a reframing-only fix, audit all title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion occurrences of “intervention,” “return,” and “training-path dependence” to ensure none claims such a comparison.
issues.evidence_needed: Either a self-contained comparator-path theorem and proof, or a claim-narrowing revision; an experiment is not required for the narrowed formal paper.
